summary: RDAP lacks queries for finding the list of domains related to entities matching a search pattern. This document defines an RDAP extension for a reverse search feature. Servers can support it based on relationships between RDAP object classes, not just the classic domain-entity case.

eli5.summary: Usually you look up a person to learn their houses. This lets you start with a person's details and list every house tied to them.

questions: how to find domains by registrant in rdap
subtitle: How an RDAP server can answer 'which domains are tied to this person or handle?' instead of only the reverse.

tldr.problem: RDAP can list the entities related to a domain, but it has no query for finding the domains related to entities that match a search pattern. Only nameserver-based reverse lookups existed.
tldr.mechanism: A new path form, {searchable-resource-type}/reverse_search/{related-resource-type}?search-condition, lets a client search one object type by properties of a related object. Servers advertise the properties they support and say which JSON members they mapped each property to, using JSONPath.
tldr.outcome: Only the entity-related searches (role, handle, fn, email) are defined, and they come with firm privacy and access-control expectations. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9536 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track) published in April 2024, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 9082 and RFC 9083 and works together with RFC 9537 in using JSONPath.

sections.title: Why Reverse Search Is Needed
sections.content:
A normal RDAP query on a domain can return the entities related to it, such as the registrant, registrar, administrative, technical or reseller contacts. The opposite direction was not allowed: a client could not ask for the domains related to an entity. Only reverse searches for the domains related to a nameserver (by ldhName or ip) existed.

The RFC points to Reverse WHOIS, a service offered by many web applications that finds domain names starting from an owner's name or email. It lists legal uses such as uncovering trademark infringements and detecting cybercrimes. Registrars may also want it, for example to resynchronize their database with the registry or to do bulk EPP updates such as changing the contacts of a set of domains.

The text answers the two classic objections to a standardized reverse search. Privacy: RDAP is built on HTTP, so it can use HTTP-based authentication and authorization. Server load: the core RDAP specifications already define search queries with similar processing needs.
sections.eli5: Normally you can ask a library which books an author wrote. Here you could not ask the opposite question. This document adds the missing question, with rules about who may ask it.

sections.title: The Reverse Search Path
sections.content:
A reverse search path has the form {searchable-resource-type}/reverse_search/{related-resource-type}?<search-condition>. The searchable type is what you get back, and the related type is what you match on.

  • searchable-resource-type: one of the search types from RFC 9082 (domains, nameservers, entities) or a resource type extension.
  • related-resource-type: one of the lookup types from RFC 9082 (domain, nameserver, entity, ip, autnum) or an extension.
  • search-condition: predicates written property=search pattern and joined with an ampersand.

A reverse search is defined by the triple of searchable type, related type and property, plus a mapping to the RDAP object member it examines. The mapping is a JSONPath expression (RFC 9535). Searches are registered in the 'RDAP Reverse Search' registry and mappings in the 'RDAP Reverse Search Mapping' registry. Two registries exist because one search may rely on different members depending on server configuration.

Although the grammar allows many related types, the only reverse searches defined here use entity as the related type. Servers MUST NOT provide reverse searches or mappings that are not registered with IANA.
sections.eli5: The address says what you want back (houses) and what you know about them (the owner). You write both in the address, then add the clues you are matching.

sections.title: Entity-Based Searches
sections.content:
Because an entity can be related to any RDAP object, the common reverse search is by entity details. Servers SHOULD support four properties for the domains, nameservers and entities searchable types with the entity related type: role, handle, fn and email.

A predicate on role means the response's roles property MUST contain at least the specified role. The fn and email properties come from the jCard of the entity, but the field references point to vCard, since jCard is just the JSON format for vCard.

Examples from the RFC include /domains/reverse_search/entity?handle=CID-40*&role=technical and /domains/reverse_search/entity?fn=Bobby*&role=registrant.
sections.eli5: You can search by who the owner is, what their ID is, their name, their email, or what job they have for the domain, like technical contact.

sections.title: Discovery, Mapping and Query Processing
sections.content:
Servers declare what they support by adding a reverse_search_properties member to the help response. Each array item has searchableResourceType, relatedResourceType and property. In every reverse search response, servers MUST also add a reverse_search_properties_mapping member to the topmost object. Each item holds the property and its propertyPath, the JSONPath of the member or members used. It is in the search response rather than the help response because it can differ by query. The member MUST be included for every property used in the search. When applied to an object, the JSONPath MUST produce a list of JSON numbers or strings.

To process a search, the server returns objects of the searchable type that match every predicate. For each predicate it applies the mapping to get values and checks whether the pattern matches at least one. A pattern matches when it equals the string form of a value or matches under the partial string matching of RFC 9082. Several predicates on the same property must each be matched by the related object.

Servers MUST return HTTP 501 (Not Implemented) for unsupported reverse searches, and MAY return 400 (Bad Request) when a request breaks local policy on how predicates combine. Responses use the formats of RFC 9083, and servers MUST put reverse_search in rdapConformance of the help response and of any response carrying the mapping member.
sections.eli5: The server posts a menu of searches it allows. When it answers, it also says which fields it looked in. If you ask for something not on the menu, it says it cannot do that.

sections.title: Privacy and Implementation Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC says operators should check whether their legal environment permits this feature. Where it uses sensitive information, that information MUST be accessible only to authorized users under a lawful basis. Because requests and responses could contain personally identifiable information, reverse search MUST be available over HTTPS only. The threats named are correlation, disclosure and misuse of data.

On cost, servers are RECOMMENDED to use indexes or similar techniques. Other mitigations are the ones used for standard searches: restricting the search functionality, rate limiting according to the user's authorization, truncating and paging results (RFC 8977), and partial responses (RFC 8982).
sections.eli5: Looking up all of someone's property is sensitive, so only trusted people should be allowed, over a private connection. The server should also be built so these searches do not slow everyone down.

sections.title: Access Control
sections.content:
Security services for controlled access are those described in RFC 7481. Providers may also route reverse search endpoints through a proxy to a dedicated backend, with digital certificates and IP allow-listing. Because the relationship is in the path, servers can set different authorization policies per relationship.

Appendix A lists access control paradigms built on OpenID Connect: role-based (RBAC), purpose-based (PBAC), attribute-based (ABAC) and time-based (TBAC). It describes two trust approaches. Full Trust relies on accredited users, optionally stating a purpose. Zero Trust requires documents showing the requestor may submit a given request, with a temporary account tied to it. The RFC suggests Full Trust for users acting in the public interest or registrars searching their own domains, and Zero Trust for domain dispute resolution providers.
sections.eli5: Some people, like a registrar looking at its own customers, can simply be trusted. Others must show paperwork first. Different people get different keys.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the extension identifier reverse_search in the 'RDAP Extensions' registry, for both URI path segments and response extensions. It also created the 'RDAP Reverse Search' and 'RDAP Reverse Search Mapping' registries under Specification Required.

New searches should not duplicate functionality available elsewhere. Additional mappings for an existing property may be registered, but all mappings of one property MUST point to response fields with the same meaning. The initial entries are the four properties fn, handle, email and role, with their JSONPath mappings.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of allowed searches and where each one looks. New ones must be added to the list so everyone agrees on what they mean.

cells: Registry trusts an accredited user, who may state a purpose
Public interest tasks, registrars on their own domains
Requestor shows documents and gets a temporary account tied to the request
